newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - India broadcast bill raises heat and dust.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - India broadcast bill raises heat and dust.

text.p: While India's six-year-old economic reform programme has meant a welcome with open arms for hordes of new industries, foreign investors are realising that broadcasting is a totally different ball game.

After years of intense debate, India's ruling centre-left coalition put a broadcasting bill before parliament in May which would end the state monopoly on radio and television and usher in regulated competition on the airwaves.
But officials have built into the Broadcast Bill a minefield of restrictions, which have irked foreign investors and puzzled domestic publishers raring to capture virgin pastures.
"What it has gone and done is open up a can of worms," an industry official said.

Critics say the bill is the handiwork of entrenched domestic business interests. The government says it has an open mind to change the bill's provisions before its planned passage in parliament later this year.
MINEFIELD OF RESTRICTIONS SPARKS HEATED DEBATE
The bill currently being considered by a multi-party committee of lawmakers has sparked fierce lobbying and a debate on issues like cultural invasion and economic interests.

"This is the first bill in 50 years of India's independence which has attracted so much attention," Subhash Chandra, who heads Zee Telefilms and runs its affiliate, Zee satellite channel, told a seminar on the Broadcast Bill recently.
Some of the main controversial restrictions in the bill are:
--Companies will need licences to operate in the sector.
--Separate licences for terrestrial broadcasters, local cable channels, satellite broadcasters operating through cable networks, and direct-to-home (DTH) satellite broadcasts.
--"Cross-service" curbs which would bar firms from taking up licences for more than one category of broadcasts -- terrestrial, local cable, satellite cable and DTH broadcasts.
--A total bar on foreign equity in terrestrial broadcasting.
--A 49 percent ceiling on foreign equity in firms eligible for satellite broadcast licences.
--"Cross media" restrictions, which would limit a newspaper owner to 20 percent equity in broadcast firms and broadcast firms to 20 percent equity in newspaper publishing firms.
--Compulsory "uplinking", or beaming of signals, from Indian soil except for during a brief transitional phase.
Analysts say the Hindi-language Zee, the current satellite market leader, could gain if the bill is passed in its current form, as it faces a relatively small number of curbs.
But even Chandra of Zee Telefilms says he is not happy with the restrictions in the proposed bill. "The cross media sections are basically defying the global trend of integration," he said.
LICENCE TO CONTROL
Foreign investors say satellite television is largely unlicensed in most parts of the world.

"The bill seeks to license something which is not a scarce resource," said Urmila Gupta, executive director of News Television India, the local arm of media baron Rupert Murdoch's Hong Kong-based Star Television told Reuters.
Star has led a host of satellite channels which have been beaming from abroad into Indian homes for six years through cable networks, without any government regulation or licensing.
Foreign broadcasters say they already face tough competition from decades-old Doordarshan, the state-run television unit which has a 70 percent market reach.
In 1995, Doordarshan accounted for television advertisement spending worth 7.5 billion rupees ($209 million) out of total adverts expenditure of 11.5 billion ($321 million).
Of the remaining expenditure on satellite television, Indian-language broadcasters account for the bulk.
Industry officials see a big future opportunity linked to high economic growth.

U.S. ambassador Frank Wisner prompted hostile media write-ups when he met Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy this year to discuss the bill, which could hurt the interests of General Electric Company's NBC, Murdoch's Star and channels like Discovery, a unit of Liberty Media Corporation.
MURDOCH FACES CURBS

The bill hit Star just when it was starting an ambitious $500 million investment to launch a direct-to-home service, which would enable homes to use small dish antennae and receive targeted packages containing dozens of channels.

Star is irked because under the provisions of the bill, it has to choose between its planned DTH service and continuing its current free-to-air satellite channel distributed through cable operators using large dish antennae.
"I have not seen a similar set of prohibitions (elsewhere)," Monroe Price, director of a programme on broadcast law at Oxford University, told Reuters.
The 49 percent cap on foreign equity is another matter of concern for foreign broadcasters.
They say such limits only help the government bureaucracy and skilful middlemen who could manipulate officials. "It could mean corruption with a capital C," said an industry official.
Cross-media restrictions have upset groups like the Times of India's publisher, Bennett, Coleman and Company, which was eyeing a big chance in television.
Arun Arora, the Times publisher's executive director, said India had 50 million homes with television sets of which 18 million had some access to satellite television.
The total circulation of the top 10 newspapers was less than seven million, he said.
"And still we hear opinions on the dangers of cross- media ownership," he said in a recent speech.
DOUBTFUL PRECEDENTS

The government says it is only following foreign -- mainly European -- precedents. "Whether in respect of foreign equity or in regard to cross-media holding, none of them is an indigenous idea," minister Reddy said.
But critics say many of the precedents have been changed in the countries where they originated. They say audience market share has emerged as a more reliable measure of monopolies.
"Ownership has not been a good way of preserving cultural values," Price of Oxford University said. "There is no intrinsic relationship between ownership and attitude towards programming."

"One provision is very troublesome -- the requirement that uplinking facilities be in this country," Reed Hundt, chairman of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission, said during a recent visit to India.
Broadcasters like Discovery channel are upset because this move would affect their plans to capture a wide Asian market from one centre.
The government says it has an open mind, but asserts that media is not just another industry to be liberalised.
"Information products are qualitatively different from any other product," Reddy said. ($1=35.8 rupees)
